clue.text: Booth with a couple of silly creatures in?

parts.note: two asses, the proverbially silly animals
taken as written

explanation.surface: A stall or booth housing a pair of foolish animals, like a petting zoo exhibit.
explanation.walkthrough: Booth looks like a stall, but it is John Wilkes Booth, who shot Abraham Lincoln in 1865; the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: John Wilkes Booth murdered President Lincoln, so he is an example of a political killer.

clue.text: Was he a politician before becoming a physicist?

parts.note: taken as written
Member of Parliament
an old poetic word for before

explanation.surface: A question about whether some scientist began his career in parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'a politician before' as the letters, then asks which physicist results.
explanation.definitionFit: André-Marie Ampère was the French scientist who founded electrodynamics; the unit of electric current is named after him.

clue.text: Spray presented by tenor after turn

indicators.note: one piece comes after the other, fixing which is written first

parts.note: a spin is a turn or twirl
the tenor of a speech is its general gist or thrust

explanation.surface: A singer, a tenor, offers a bouquet after taking his turn on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tenor' looks like a singer, but it means the general sense of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Spindrift is the fine sea spray blown off wave crests by strong wind.

clue.text: A man of letters, the gipsy Lavengro

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a learned, bookish person
second meaning: Lavengro, hero of George Borrow's novel, was a learned man living among Romany travellers, a figure also echoed in Arnold's poem about a gipsy

explanation.walkthrough: Lavengro is Romany for 'word-master', the name Borrow's gipsy friends gave his bookish hero; Matthew Arnold's poem 'The Scholar-Gipsy' tells of a similar Oxford student.
explanation.definitionFit: A learned academic is a person of letters, and Borrow's Lavengro is the classic literary example of a learned wanderer.

clue.text: Prisoner inside is making representations

indicators.note: the first piece sits within the second word

parts.note: taken as written
a con is a convict

explanation.surface: An inmate in jail is busy producing pictures or statements.
explanation.definitionFit: Icons are images or likenesses, especially religious portraits, so they are depictions of something.

clue.text: He accompanies an Aberdonian, say, across a river

indicators.note: one piece stretches across the other, so it sits on either side of it

parts.note: an East Scot: Aberdeen is on Scotland's east coast, so E plus SCOT
R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A man accompanies a fellow from Aberdeen as they cross a river together.
explanation.walkthrough: Aberdeen is a city on the north-east coast of Scotland, so an Aberdonian is an East Scot; the river letter goes inside the Scot.
explanation.definitionFit: A man who goes along with someone, as guard or partner for an evening, is that person's companion or chaperone.

clue.text: Like a burlesque thus including send-up of a woman

indicators.note: one word includes the other, holding it inside

parts.note: Latin for thus, used to flag a quoted error

indicators.note: in a down clue sending something up turns it bottom to top

parts.note: a woman's name

explanation.surface: Mocking like a stage burlesque, a sketch that sends up a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send-up' suits the parody of the surface, but it is the signal to read the name upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A burlesque mocks its subject by grotesque imitation, which is exactly what mocking satirical writing does.

clue.text: Bluish gas — a lightweight one

parts.note: an ounce, abbreviated oz, is a small weight
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pale blue gas described as an unusually light one.
explanation.definitionFit: Ozone, the three-atom form of oxygen, is a pale blue gas with a sharp smell.

clue.text: Islander a painter depicted astride a horse

indicators.note: a rider astride has a leg on each side, so the painter sits around the other letters

parts.note: the Venetian Renaissance master
a plus H, slang for heroin, which is also called horse

explanation.surface: A native of some island painted by an artist on horseback.
explanation.walkthrough: Horse is drug slang for heroin, whose abbreviation is H. Gauguin famously painted Tahitians, which makes the surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Tahiti in French Polynesia is an inhabitant of a Pacific island.

clue.text: So depict characters like Attila the Hun

indicators.note: the clue invites us to treat the words purely as a set of letters to be laid out afresh

parts.note: eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to portray figures such as the brutal ruler of the Huns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' looks like people in a drama, but it means the letters of the preceding words.
explanation.definitionFit: Attila ruled the Huns as an absolute and ruthless tyrant, the model of a tyrannical autocrat.

clue.text: Promise to make jam, others not being involved

indicators.note: letters that are involved are tangled together and come out in a new order

parts.note: a jam is a fix or predicament
these nine letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A pledge to make jam, with nobody else being drawn into the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jam' looks like preserves, but it is a tight spot. Troth is an old word for faith or loyalty, as in the wedding vow.
explanation.definitionFit: To plight one's troth is the old phrase for pledging faithfulness, especially in agreeing to marry, so it means to give a solemn word.

clue.text: Solves puzzles

definitions.meaning: first meaning: as a verb, to riddle is to work out or interpret a puzzle
second meaning: as a noun, enigmas or conundrums

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence about solving, but the first word is a verb and the second a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the verb for interpreting an enigma and the plural noun naming such enigmas themselves.

clue.text: Warning compelling king to intervene

indicators.note: something that intervenes steps in between, so it goes into the middle of the other word

parts.note: a compelling argument is a powerful one
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A stern warning that obliges a monarch to step into some dispute.
explanation.definitionFit: An omen or sign that something bad is coming serves as a forewarning or ominous signal.

clue.text: Military Intelligence doctor developing tiny photograph

indicators.note: something developing is changing shape, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: the usual abbreviation, as in MI5
these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: An army spy doctor is developing film of a minute spy photograph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Developing' suits a photograph in the surface, but it is the signal to rearrange the doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: A microdot is a photograph shrunk to the size of a full stop, a classic espionage device for hiding documents.

clue.text: US infantryman in a stew?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: American slang for a foot soldier, especially in the First World War
second meaning: a dumpling, something found floating in a casserole

explanation.walkthrough: 'In a stew' suggests a soldier in trouble, but the second sense is literal: a boiled dumpling cooked in stew. The question mark marks the definition by description.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is American slang for a First World War foot soldier and also names a boiled flour dumpling.

clue.text: Fellow graduate accommodates Head of Maths for short break

parts.note: the prefix co- marks a fellow, as in co-worker

indicators.note: to accommodate is to give room inside, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: Master of Arts

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the subject

explanation.surface: A fellow alumnus puts up the head of the maths department for a brief holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: A fellow graduate is a co-MA; the M from Maths goes inside that.
explanation.definitionFit: This punctuation mark signals a brief pause in a sentence, shorter than a full stop.

clue.text: Sail manufacturer grasps nothing about rigging at first

indicators.note: to grasp is to hold within, so the maker surrounds the rest

parts.note: one who manufactures something
zero, shaped like the letter
on as in a talk on a subject

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A sailmaker who has no idea about rigging at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: The three inner pieces go between the first and second letters of the maker.
explanation.definitionFit: A moonraker is a light square sail set at the very top of a mast above the skysail.

clue.text: Event raised nothing to support fellow music-maker

indicators.note: in a down clue supporting pieces sit beneath the one they hold up

parts.note: a fellow is a man
a do is a party or function

indicators.note: in a down clue raising a word lifts it so it reads from the bottom upwards

parts.note: zero

explanation.surface: A fundraising event made nothing to back a colleague who plays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' suggests money collected at the event; it is the signal to read the zero word upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandolin is a lute-like stringed instrument, so it is something that makes music.

clue.text: Greek screen with the ends missing

indicators.note: the first and last letters are lost, leaving only the interior

parts.note: a lattice is a criss-cross screen of strips

explanation.surface: A Greek screen whose edges have broken off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek' looks like the start of a description of the screen, but it is the definition: Attica is the region around Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: Attic describes things of Attica or ancient Athens, so it is an adjective for that part of Greece.

clue.text: Greek character provided quarters for Asians

parts.note: the 22nd letter of the Greek alphabet
two compass quarters, north-east and south-east

explanation.surface: A Greek man offered lodgings to some travellers from Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quarters' looks like lodgings, but it is two compass quarters.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of China are among the peoples of Asia, so they are inhabitants of that continent.

clue.text: With peacekeepers practical sense is exceptional

parts.note: United Nations forces keep the peace
British slang for common sense, as in 'use your common'

explanation.surface: Peacekeeping troops with sound practical judgement are a rarity.
explanation.walkthrough: In British colloquial speech 'common' alone can mean common sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rare and out of the ordinary is unusual, the opposite of everyday.

clue.text: The brotherhood's political beliefs?

parts.note: surface reading: the ideology of some fraternity, perhaps a socialist fellowship of workers
setter's reading: the brothers are Groucho, Chico, Harpo and their siblings, the comedy family, so their creed is the doctrine sharing their surname

explanation.walkthrough: The surname of the comic Brothers is also that of Karl, founder of communist theory.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the political and economic theory of Karl, the communist philosopher, which shares its name with the comic film brothers.

clue.text: Chaste girl digesting set novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters take a new form
something digested is taken inside, so the girl holds the other letters

parts.note: a girl's name
these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A pure-minded young woman takes in a whole set of novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set novel' sounds like a set text for study; novel is the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vestal Virgins of Rome were sworn to celibacy, so the adjective means pure or virginal.

clue.text: Muslim food King Edward V consumed

indicators.note: food that is consumed ends up inside, so the dish holds the other letters

parts.note: a dish is a serving of food
Edwardus Rex, the royal cipher
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Muslim dish eaten by the boy king Edward V.
explanation.walkthrough: King Edward is also a potato variety, which suits the food surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A dervish is a member of a Sufi Muslim religious order, famous for whirling dances.

clue.text: Put this away — at once. OK?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: put this word in front of away and the phrase means immediately

explanation.walkthrough: The first half reads as an order to tidy up, but it describes a word that with 'away' makes a phrase meaning immediately.
explanation.definitionFit: Right away means immediately, and right on its own is an exclamation of agreement like all right.

clue.text: Ferret one out for Douglas, perhaps

indicators.note: out here means disordered or awry, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone ferrets out a man called Douglas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ferret ... out' reads as a phrasal verb meaning to hunt down; Douglas is not a man but a conifer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Douglas fir is a tall North American conifer, so it is one example of this kind of evergreen.

clue.text: A female revolutionary, to begin with?

definitions.text: A female revolutionary, to begin with?

indicators.note: to begin with points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter
a red is a communist revolutionary
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman who was a radical in her early days.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read one way it describes a woman, read the other its words give her name, with A placed last.
explanation.definitionFit: Freda is a woman's first name, so the solution is one particular woman, here imagined as a youthful radical.

clue.text: Supporter's obstructionist stance resulting in dismissal

definitions.text: Supporter's obstructionist stance resulting in dismissal

parts.words: Supporter's obstructionist stance resulting in dismissal
parts.note: surface reading: a backer's stubborn position gets them sacked
setter's reading: a limb, which supports the body, stands in the way of the ball in cricket

explanation.surface: A backer takes an obstructive line and is fired for it.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a batter is out if the ball strikes their leg when it would otherwise have hit the stumps.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the cricket mode of dismissal, abbreviated lbw, for blocking the stumps with the body.

clue.text: Talk given in German at tertiary college

indicators.note: the letters are supplied within the words that follow, running across them

parts.note: the run of letters spanning these three words
surface padding, completing the picture of a tertiary college

explanation.surface: A lecture delivered in German at a further-education college.
explanation.definitionFit: To natter is to chatter or chat idly, a British informal word for conversation.

clue.text: State soldiers gatecrash dance in the castle

indicators.note: gatecrashers push their way inside an event, so these letters go into the other word

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance
MO is the abbreviation for Missouri
the Royal Artillery

explanation.surface: Soldiers from some state barge uninvited into a dance held at a castle.
explanation.definitionFit: Balmoral Castle in Aberdeenshire is the British royal family's Scottish residence.
